<reason>Both sides argued the motion as written and clashed cleanly, but A built the more durable route. A anchored on the modest burden ("hard to justify," not "ban"), then landed two damaging strikes: (1) the fork — tourism cannot be climatically trivial and simultaneously the thing amortizing reusable vehicles — and (2) the disaggregation that joyride flights are suborbital and share little with the heavy reusables that satellite constellations and government contracts actually paid for. B answered the fork plausibly by separating atmospheric totals from a firm's learning rate, but when pressed for a threshold gave "tens of flights a year," which A immediately turned: a cadence that low bends no cost curve, so B's public-benefit story shrank to fit its own emissions defence. B never engaged the suborbital/anchor-customer point with any specificity beyond asserting that "the base thickens." B's strongest work was on A's criterion — a concert is also a memory, a polar cruise's product is the sensation of being there, and aerospace factories pay wages just as ski valleys do — which genuinely dented A's attempt to acquit ordinary luxuries. But A's proportionality prong (harm relative to benefit reaching past the buyer) plus A's willingness to bite the bullet on jets and polar cruises kept the criterion coherent, and it stripped B of its main comparative shield ("those already run, so this is fine"). B's plain "no" — that unresolved climate and poverty make no expensive indulgence harder to justify — was consistent but handed A the memorable "amnesty" framing, which reads as abolishing the question rather than answering it. A's Rebuttal 2 was clipped for length, a real execution cost, but the substance was already delivered; B's repeated well-under-cap turns left live technical pressure unanswered.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's pressure question demanding a flight-rate threshold, and the follow-up: B either refused a number (conceding the fork) or named one — "tens of flights a year" — which A then used to show the industrial-base benefit is too small to justify the stratospheric harm. That trap collapsed B's innovation route.</best_rebuttal>
